title: AI and EdTech in the Early Years: Risks, Uses and What Needs to Change
label: 20 October 2026 · AI and EdTech in Early Years
summary: The Committee heard from early years practitioners, academics and advocates about how AI and other digital tools are already affecting children from birth to five. Witnesses reported real worries—more children arriving with social and emotional delays, poorly designed AI toys, and overwhelmed staff—alongside limited useful uses (administration, some assistive tech). They urged more training for educators, clearer product standards and regulation, sustained research (including long-term studies), and careful, equity-focused deployment especially for SEND and vulnerable children.

chapters.title: Who spoke and what we asked
chapters.takeaway: The Committee questioned early years leaders, digital pedagogy experts and academics about how AI and edtech affect babies, toddlers and pre-schoolers.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Today we’re focusing on AI and edtech in the early years. We’ll hear from practitioners and academics about impacts, benefits and what the Government should do.

turns.speaker: Neil Leitch
turns.text: I run the Early Years Alliance, representing about 18,000 nurseries and childminders and operating 28 settings in deprived areas, so we see development issues first hand.

turns.speaker: Professor Gibson
turns.text: I research early language, communication and social-emotional development at Cambridge. We’ve been studying AI-enabled toys and their effects on under-fives.

turns.speaker: Richard Waite
turns.text: I advise on early years digital pedagogy and safeguarding. I work with nurseries to introduce suitable tech and to help them avoid common pitfalls.

chapters.title: Everyday impacts: what is already happening
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses described more children with social and emotional delays, admin uses of AI, AI toys with unknown effects, and low staff confidence.

turns.speaker: Neil Leitch
turns.text: Post-pandemic many children arrive with social and emotional delays. Managers report violent incidents: in our 28 nurseries from Jan–Sept we logged 43 staff accidents; 19 were from children kicking, biting or pulling hair.

turns.speaker: Professor Gibson
turns.text: We observed AI-enabled cuddly toys that embed generative AI chatbots. Practitioners are worried and feel they lack the skills to judge these products. There’s very little independent evidence about developmental impact.

turns.speaker: Richard Waite
turns.text: On the ground, people assume 'technology' means screens. That fear—plus staffing and budget pressures—stops many nurseries from exploring constructive digital tools like coding toys or digital microscopes.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What are nurseries actually using now?

turns.speaker: Neil Leitch
turns.text: Mostly administrative software, some speech-and-language supports, and occasional assistive tech. But AI-generated development reports can feel cold and lack nuance, and AI-written parent letters are flooding staff with complex documents.

turns.speaker: Professor Gibson
turns.text: I’ve seen Alexa-type devices and systems used for planning. Sometimes settings use AI without realising it. The tech in practice is more educator-facing than child-facing at present.

turns.speaker: Richard Waite
turns.text: The sector needs digital pedagogy—thinking about why you use a tool, how you implement it and what impact you expect—rather than tech for tech’s sake. When used thoughtfully, tech can be another learning tool like sand or Play‑Doh.

chapters.title: Safety, parents and training
chapters.takeaway: Major concerns: product safety (especially AI toys), privacy, home influence, and lack of staff training and guidance for parents.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Has Government grasped the scale of these impacts?

turns.speaker: Neil Leitch
turns.text: No. Physical safeguarding gets quick attention, but emotional safeguarding does not. Educators are trusted by families and could help parents, but they lack training in AI, cyber-security and how to respond when things go wrong.

turns.speaker: Professor Gibson
turns.text: We need cross‑sector working—health, social services and education—and psychological safety in product standards for toys with generative AI. Friendship‑affirming AI can be risky when a child is developmentally vulnerable.

turns.speaker: Richard Waite
turns.text: Training and CPD are the big gaps. A sector survey showed 46% use AI, 31% have guidance but only 21% have training. Apprentices and managers often get no support on digital pedagogy or cyber-security.

turns.speaker: Caroline Voaden
turns.text: Parents and nurseries are anxious about photos and online exposure; some nurseries are removing faces from marketing because images can be misused by AI.

turns.speaker: Richard Waite
turns.text: Private, secure photo-sharing platforms for parents exist, but public advertising raises real safeguarding fears. The sector is reacting by limiting images, which is a shame for parent engagement.

turns.speaker: Professor Gibson
turns.text: There have been toys that said inappropriate things—poorly guarded generative models. Without product regulation on guardrails, risks will grow as global products arrive in the market.

chapters.title: Evidence, research and regulation
chapters.takeaway: There’s little long-term research; witnesses recommended big, longitudinal studies, procurement standards, and risk‑based regulation tied to safeguarding.

turns.speaker: Professor Leaton Gray
turns.text: We have small short‑term studies but almost no long-view evidence. Government spending favours rollout over evaluation. We need longitudinal research tracking cohorts through childhood and adolescence to see lifelong effects.

turns.speaker: Professor Blakemore
turns.text: High-quality research takes years but AI moves faster. Still, we can apply what we already know about brain development: childhood is highly plastic and social interaction with real people is crucial—AI may alter that input.

turns.speaker: Dr Aitken
turns.text: Don’t be driven by hype or commercial pitches. Start by identifying specific teaching problems that need solving; often AI won’t be the right solution. Products should be developed with education expertise and child-centred design.

turns.speaker: Meg Moss
turns.text: Regulation should be proportional but risk‑stratified: therapeutic or emotionally-supportive AI is high-risk and needs stricter oversight. We also need public awareness campaigns about limits and harms of AI.

turns.speaker: Mark Sewards
turns.text: How long will useful research take?

turns.speaker: Professor Leaton Gray
turns.text: To understand effects across schooling and into early adulthood we need studies running years or decades, not just weeks or months. Short trials are useful but don’t answer long-term questions.

turns.speaker: Neil Leitch
turns.text: We should also have product accountability—companies making edtech should answer to a body that understands child development, like medical devices do for healthcare.

turns.speaker: Professor Blakemore
turns.text: And we must recognise products can do harm, not just fail to help—so safety assessments are essential before wide adoption, especially with children.

chapters.title: Inclusion, SEND and classroom practice
chapters.takeaway: AI can help with assistive tech and personalised support, but it risks entrenching inequalities, misdiagnosis, and replacing crucial teacher judgement and social practice.

turns.speaker: Mark Sewards
turns.text: Can AI close gaps for children with SEND?

turns.speaker: Professor Gibson
turns.text: There’s hope—AI can help profiling and identify needs—but the evidence is thin. Tools must be co-designed with families and specialists. Off‑the‑shelf products are unlikely to be adequate.

turns.speaker: Neil Leitch
turns.text: I’m hopeful but cautious. Policy and inspection focus have driven inclusion more than edtech. I saw promising products in China, but settings avoid risky tech because of fear and poor support.

turns.speaker: Richard Waite
turns.text: Assistive tech can transform a child’s experience—tablets, larger buttons, specialised mice can include a child in nursery life—but procuring the right device and training staff made the difference in my example.

turns.speaker: Jodie Gosling
turns.text: What about AI tutors and personalised learning—do they change teacher-pupil relationships?

turns.speaker: Dr Aitken
turns.text: AI tutors can augment teachers but not replace teacher judgement. Risks include privacy, inaccuracy and unequal access. Children also use general chatbots as companions; those can be sycophantic and reinforce bad ideas.

turns.speaker: Professor Blakemore
turns.text: Human teachers pick up non-verbal cues and welfare concerns AI misses. Social skills—oracy, teamwork, dealing with friction—must be practised with people, not bots.

turns.speaker: Sureena Brackenridge
turns.text: For SEND, how do we avoid bias in systems?

turns.speaker: Professor Leaton Gray
turns.text: Avoid simplistic labels—SEND does not automatically mean cognitive impairment. Systems must be bespoke and not create a two‑tier solution where 'those children' get automated help while others get real teaching.

turns.speaker: Meg Moss
turns.text: Some AI tools model neurodivergence from a deficit view, which can be harmful. We need careful design, oversight and a role for human specialists.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: To close: what concrete next steps did witnesses recommend?

turns.speaker: Professor Leaton Gray
turns.text: Urgent: cross-Department coordination (DfE, DCMS, regulators), risk‑stratified standards, procurement guidance, and long-term cohort research.

turns.speaker: Dr Aitken
turns.text: Start interventions from needs, not tech hype; support educator training; build product labelling or simple standards so settings can judge safety and suitability.

turns.speaker: Neil Leitch
turns.text: Make AI and emotional safeguarding part of training, support parents, and ensure early years staff are funded and given time for CPD on digital issues.

turns.speaker: Richard Waite
turns.text: Provide practical CPD, model lesson plans showing intent/implementation/impact for digital pedagogy, and help nurseries access the right, affordable tools.

turns.speaker: Professor Blakemore
turns.text: Protect time and space for human social interaction and oracy in early education—those are developmentally essential and not replaceable by AI.
